name: libbf
baseline: GMP 6.3 / MPFR 4.2 (timed through the Rust rug 1.30.0 crate)
workload: Correctly rounded floating-point multiply at 300,000-bit precision, measured as ns per 64-bit limb, from a third-party benchmark of Bellard's libbf C library against rug (GMP/MPFR) on one machine.
claimed_speedup: Only one win in the data: mul at 300,000 bits is 51.2 ns/limb for libbf versus 78.9 ns/limb for rug, about 1.5x faster (derived from page data). Not faster elsewhere: mul at 3,000 bits 13.0 vs 9.4 and at 30,000 bits 43.0 vs 35.3; add at 300,000 bits 1.1 vs 0.4; div 485.2 vs 187.0; sqrt 464.1 vs 139.2; transcendentals about 3-5x slower than MPFR.
compiler_and_flags: libbf C version 2025-06-03, prebuilt bftest built with clang -O2; rug 1.30.0 (gmp-mpfr-sys 1.7.1 -> GMP 6.3, MPFR 4.2) under rustc 1.96.1 --release
stars_or_usage: 19 stars (rurban mirror of Fabrice Bellard's libbf tar releases; libbf is also embedded in QuickJS)
tradeoffs: Small library for binary and decimal arbitrary-precision floating point with NTT multiplication and Newton division/sqrt; transcendental functions are not speed-optimized; add, div, sqrt and the elementary functions are slower than GMP/MPFR.
caveats: Evidence for an already catalogued project, and mixed: libbf beats rug only for large multiplications (300,000 bits) in this data. The benchmark belongs to libbeef, a Rust port of libbf, and was written by its author as a side comparison. libbf was timed by its own bftest harness, rug by the Rust harness in a different process; operand distributions differ (libbf uses run-length random bits with sizes uniform in [1, 2*prec], rug uses full-width prec-bit operands), so the 300,000-bit win may partly be an input artifact. The libbf README itself says 'It is not the fastest library nor the smallest'. The rurban repo is a mirror, the upstream is bellard.org/libbf (not opened, host not reachable here). Numbers come from the report page I opened; I did not run anything.
found_via: Blogs / talks: WebSearch 'Bellard libbf arbitrary precision floating point benchmark compared to MPFR' surfaced lifthrasiir/libbeef docs/benchmark-report.md

name: mp++
baseline: GMP 6.2.0 (mpz_t, benchmarked through Boost.Multiprecision gmp_int calling the GMP API directly)
workload: Vectors of 3x10^7 random small integers (1-limb static size, unsigned and signed, also 2-limb): dot product, element-wise multiply-add, division, GCD, LCM, left shift, conversion and sorting, mp++ integer vs GMP, Boost cpp_int, FLINT fmpzxx and builtin 64/128-bit integers.
claimed_speedup: Docs: 1-limb unsigned dot product 'mp++ is almost 4 times faster than GMP'; vector multiply-add 'more than 7 times faster than GMP'; vector division 'mp++ and FLINT ... are about 8 times faster than GMP'. Slowdown versus builtin 64-bit integers is x4 (dot product), less than x3 (multiply-add).
compiler_and_flags: Per doc/benchmarks.rst: GCC 10.1 with mp++ 0.21, GMP 6.2.0, Boost 1.73.0, FLINT 2.5.2; the benchmark CMake target uses the project's Release flags (CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE defaults to Release), exact flag values not quoted in the docs
tradeoffs: C++ library layered on GMP/MPFR/MPC; the win comes from the small-value optimization (values up to a fixed number of limbs live inline, no heap allocation), so it applies to 1-2 limb operands and large operands defer to GMP speed.
caveats: Evidence upgrade for a catalogued project (is_evidence_for_known): the earlier record had no hardware or compiler. Results were last updated 2020-06-09 and the Ryzen 3950x and GCC 10.1 are old; the benchmarks only cover 1-limb and 2-limb integers, the regime where GMP's fixed per-object overhead dominates. Build flags come from the CMake Release default rather than being listed in the docs.
found_via: GitHub: raw doc/benchmarks.rst and doc/integer_benchmarks.rst in bluescarni/mppp, opened while checking the mp++ record

name: PocketFFT (C++ header-only), independent benchmark
baseline: KissFFT (also FFTW_ESTIMATE and FFTW_MEASURE, Intel MKL as reference)
workload: Independent shootout by the project-gemmi author: 1D complex and real transforms, 2D, and 3D complex-to-complex and real-to-complex (256^3 and other sizes), single precision except the C pocketfft in the 1D tables, timed with their own benchmark programs.
claimed_speedup: 3D c2c 256x256x256: pocketfft 264 ms vs KissFFT 785 ms, FFTW est. 730 ms, FFTW meas. 162 ms, MKL 155 ms. 3D r2c 256x256x256: pocketfft AVX 97 ms vs KissFFT 436 ms, FFTW est. 219 ms, FFTW meas. 98 ms, MKL 61 ms. 1D c2c n=512 with SIMD disabled: pocketfft 4009 ns vs KissFFT 6553 ns. Plan creation n=512: pocketfft 1274 ns vs FFTW meas. 25610 ns. Ratios (derived from page data): about 3.0x over KissFFT on 3D c2c, 4.5x on 3D r2c, 1.6x on 1D c2c without SIMD; parity with FFTW_MEASURE on 3D r2c with AVX; slower than FFTW_MEASURE and MKL on 3D c2c.
compiler_and_flags: GCC 8 -O3 (Clang 8 also tried; the page says pocketfft is about 12% faster with Clang 8)
hardware: Intel Core i7-5600U (listing shows 4 CPUs at 3200 MHz; L1d 32K x2, L2 256K x2, L3 4096K)
stars_or_usage: 158 stars (mreineck/pocketfft); the gemmi README says NumPy (from 1.17) and SciPy (from 1.4.0) adopted PocketFFT
tradeoffs: Vectorizes only multi-dimensional transforms or batches of 1D transforms, and uses GCC/Clang vector extensions rather than intrinsics, so top speed needs GCC or Clang. Very cheap plan creation and a small header-only footprint.
caveats: Evidence for an already catalogued project (is_evidence_for_known). Benchmark repo last updated 2022-06-21 on a 2015 laptop CPU; the 1D tables use the double-precision C pocketfft against single-precision rivals, and the author was migrating to the cpp branch. The compiler is stated in the 1D section, not repeated for every 3D table. FFTW was Ubuntu 18.04 binaries, not rebuilt. Against FFTW_MEASURE and MKL pocketfft is slower or at parity, so the clear win is over KissFFT and FFTW_ESTIMATE.
found_via: Blogs / talks: WebSearch 'FFT library faster than FFTW and Intel MKL benchmark AVX-512 NEON github C++ header-only' surfaced project-gemmi/benchmarking-fft

name: muFFT, independent benchmark
workload: Independent shootout by the project-gemmi author: single-precision 1D complex and real-to-complex transforms (n=256..512) and 2D complex 256x256, with SIMD enabled and disabled.
claimed_speedup: 2D c2c 256x256: mufft 259 us vs FFTW est. 1197 us and FFTW meas. 306 us. 1D r2c n=512: mufft 511 ns vs FFTW est. 814 ns and FFTW meas. 681 ns. Ratios (derived from page data): 4.6x and 1.18x on 2D c2c; 1.59x and 1.33x on 1D r2c. On 1D c2c muFFT is slower than FFTW_MEASURE (n=256: 325 vs 274 ns; n=512: 719 vs 588 ns) and about level with FFTW_ESTIMATE.
tradeoffs: Only 1D and 2D transforms, sizes limited to what its radix codelets support (the shootout shows n/a for n=384, 480 and 480x480), no 3D, single precision only in the shootout's feature table. Separate no-SIMD, SSE, SSE3 and AVX codelets, about 80 kB of binary.
caveats: Evidence for an already catalogued project (is_evidence_for_known). Mixed result: wins over FFTW on 2D c2c 256x256 and 1D r2c n=512 but loses to FFTW_MEASURE on 1D c2c. 2015-era laptop CPU, benchmark repo last touched 2022-06-21, FFTW from Ubuntu 18.04 binaries. The GitHub page lists both MIT and GPL-2.0, so check which files carry the GPL before copying.
found_via: Blogs / talks: WebSearch 'FFT library faster than FFTW and Intel MKL benchmark AVX-512 NEON github C++ header-only' surfaced project-gemmi/benchmarking-fft

name: PFFFT (per-CPU benchmark results by hayguen/pffft_benchmarks)
workload: Single-precision 1-D complex and real FFTs of power-of-two sizes 16 to 1,048,576 with SIMD, in MFLOPS (5*N*log2(N) for complex, 2.5*N*log2(N) for real), on an Intel Xeon Gold 6130 with gcc 8.3.0; the repo holds 20+ per-CPU result files (ARM Cortex-A9/A15, Raspberry Pi 3B+/4B, Atom N270, Core 2, i5/i7 generations, Apple A8X).
claimed_speedup: Xeon Gold 6130, complex single precision: PFFFT (ordered) vs KissFFT at N=1,024 21,283 vs 5,184 MFLOPS (4.1x, relative duration column 4.106) and at N=1,048,576 11,230 vs 2,390 (4.7x); real N=1,024 24,027 vs 4,247 (5.7x). Vs FFTW: FFTW(auto) is faster on complex (N=1,024 49,696 MFLOPS vs PFFFT 21,283), PFFFT wins only at N>=524,288 against FFTW(estim) (N=1,048,576 11,230 vs 5,719 MFLOPS, 1.96x derived from page data); on real data PFFFT is about even to 8% faster than FFTW(auto) at N=512 to 2,048 (relative duration of FFTW(auto) 1.014, 1.078, 1.005) and the unordered PFFFT-U has a 10-17% shorter duration than ordered PFFFT at N=64 to 2,048 (relative duration 0.83 to 0.92).
compiler_and_flags: gcc 8.3.0 per the file name; optimisation flags not stated in the results file (the benchmark CMake uses -DBENCH_ARCH=native per hayguen/pffft README)
tradeoffs: Licence is described as BSD-like with no SPDX id in the READMEs (LICENSE.txt in hayguen/pffft). Single-precision 1-D only in the original; sizes must be multiples of 16 (complex) or 32 (real) with SIMD; the benchmarks use the ordered transform for PFFFT and report the faster unordered variant separately.
caveats: Evidence for an already-catalogued project (marton78/pffft). The results are tables and plots from the pffft fork maintainer, not a neutral third party, and the results file does not state compiler flags. FFTW(auto) is recorded as 0.000000 for N>=4096 (not measured), so the FFTW comparison above 2,048 rests on FFTW(estim). FFTW is clearly faster than PFFFT on complex data up to about 262,144 points, which fits the README's own statement that PFFFT aims to be at least 50% as fast as the fastest FFT.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): https://github.com/hayguen/pffft_benchmarks (found via web search 'hayguen pffft_benchmarks results'); file list from https://github.com/hayguen/pffft_benchmarks/tree/master

name: cpp-random-benchmarks (zeFresk PRNG shootout)
baseline: std::mt19937 (and std::mt19937_64, C rand(), std::minstd_rand, std::ranlux engines in the same table)
workload: Mean time per generated random value for about 40 C++ PRNG engines, 100 benchmark repetitions each (--benchmark_repetitions=100), code written to stop the compiler optimizing the generation away.
claimed_speedup: Results table: xoshiro256++ 1.06 ns and pcg_cpp::pcg32_fast 0.933 ns vs std::mt19937 3.70 ns and std::mt19937_64 3.40 ns (about 3.5x and 4.0x faster than mt19937, derived from page data); pcg_cpp::pcg32 1.09 ns, pcg_cpp::pcg64 1.98 ns, pcg_cpp::pcg64_fast 1.31 ns, wjakob pcg32 1.06 ns, C rand() 15.4 ns.
tradeoffs: Benchmark harness only (CMake, include/, src/); the engines it times are third-party. AGPL-3.0 harness licence, though the winners it identifies have their own licences.
caveats: Shootout whose winners are already catalogued: xoshiro256++ links to david-cortes/xoshiro_cpp, the pcg_cpp rows link to imneme/pcg-cpp and the wjakob rows to wjakob/pcg32, so this is Tier A evidence for known projects (is_evidence_for_known) rather than a new library. Ivy Bridge i5-3570 is an old CPU without AVX2, so ratios may differ on current hardware. Standard-library implementation (libstdc++ or libc++) is not stated. The README remark that pcg32_8 is fastest 'if your CPU have AVX' was not measured on that machine.
found_via: WebSearch query 'Efficiently generating a random number in a range bounded-rands benchmark C++ blog' (result 'cpp random benchmarks'), then github.com repo page and README.adoc via raw.githubusercontent.com

name: cpp-random-benchmarks (PCG and xoshiro vs std::mt19937 shootout)
baseline: std::mt19937 and std::mt19937_64 (also std::minstd_rand, ranlux24/48, knuth_b and rand())
workload: Mean time per generated number (Google Benchmark, 100 repetitions) for xoshiro, pcg-cpp, wjakob pcg32, Jenkins small PRNG, rand() and the std engines.
claimed_speedup: README table: xoshiro256++ 1.06 ns (946.7M/s) and pcg32_fast 0.933 ns (1071.97M/s) vs std::mt19937_64 3.40 ns (294.3M/s) and std::mt19937 3.70 ns (270.7M/s), about 3.2x and 4.0x (derived from page data); pcg32 1.09 ns, pcg64_fast 1.31 ns, pcg64 1.98 ns, std::ranlux48 98.3 ns, rand() 15.4 ns.
tradeoffs: A benchmark harness, not a library; CMake downloads the engines from their own repos. Winners are projects already catalogued (imneme/pcg-cpp, prng.di.unimi.it xoshiro, wjakob/pcg32).
caveats: Reported as third-party Tier A evidence for already-known projects (pcg-cpp, xoshiro, wjakob pcg32). Builds without -march=native, so the AVX pcg32_8 variant was not measured; standard library behind the clang build is not stated; 2012-era CPU. AGPL-3.0 applies to the harness.
found_via: WebSearch: 'C++ SIMD random number generator faster than xoshiro PCG benchmark github' (zeFresk/cpp-random-benchmarks listed); opened the repo page (README.adoc text) and commits page.

name: xoshiro256++ via david-cortes/xoshiro_cpp, as measured in zeFresk/cpp-random-benchmarks
baseline: std::mt19937_64 (also std::mt19937, std::minstd_rand, std::ranlux48, C rand())
workload: Mean time per generated 64-bit value, Google Benchmark, 100 repetitions, code written to prevent compiler tricks; about 20 generators compared.
claimed_speedup: xoshiro256++ 1.06 ns +/- 0.002 (946.7M/s) vs std::mt19937_64 3.40 ns +/- 0.028 (294.3M/s) and std::mt19937 3.70 ns (about 3.2x, derived from page data); README labels it 'Fastest for 64 bits, good quality'.
tradeoffs: The wrapper makes xoshiro256++ and xoshiro128++ usable with <random> distributions, jump and state serialization; the repo's seeding differs slightly from Vigna's original.
caveats: Evidence for an already catalogued project (prng.di.unimi.it is on the known list); reported as is_evidence_for_known. The benchmark repo (zeFresk/cpp-random-benchmarks) is AGPL-3.0, last commit 2023-06-08, no SIMD flags, standard library unstated, old 2012 CPU. The wrapper repo's own last commit date and stars were not re-checked for this entry (1 star seen).
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): WebSearch 'github PRNG shootout benchmark C++ xoshiro256 PCG64 sfc64 romu wyrand speed table' surfaced zeFresk/cpp-random-benchmarks; README.adoc opened and its table quoted.

name: PCG (pcg_cpp::pcg32_fast and others) as measured in zeFresk/cpp-random-benchmarks
baseline: std::mt19937 and std::mt19937_64 (also std::minstd_rand, std::ranlux48, C rand())
workload: Mean time per generated value, Google Benchmark, 100 repetitions, about 20 generators compared.
claimed_speedup: pcg_cpp::pcg32_fast 0.933 ns +/- 0.006 (1071.97M/s) vs std::mt19937 3.70 ns +/- 0.048 (270.65M/s), about 4.0x (derived from page data); pcg32 1.09 ns; pcg64_fast 1.31 ns and pcg64 1.98 ns vs std::mt19937_64 3.40 ns (2.6x and 1.7x, derived). README: 'PCG is superior in all aspects for non-cryptographic uses'.
tradeoffs: PCG variants differ in state size and speed (pcg32_fast is the fastest 32-bit variant here, pcg64 the slowest 64-bit one in this table); the same table also lists wjakob pcg32 (1.06 ns) and pcg32_8 (8.48 ns, AVX path not usable on this CPU).
caveats: Evidence for an already catalogued project (imneme/pcg-cpp is on the known list); reported as is_evidence_for_known. Same single-CPU, standard-library-unstated benchmark as the xoshiro entry; zeFresk benchmark repo is AGPL-3.0 and has not been updated since 2023-06-08. Last commit date of pcg-cpp not re-checked for this entry.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): WebSearch 'github PRNG shootout benchmark C++ xoshiro256 PCG64 sfc64 romu wyrand speed table' surfaced zeFresk/cpp-random-benchmarks; README.adoc opened and its table quoted.
